entries.question: Alec controls [Elspeth Conquers Death] and puts the third lore counter it. With the triggered ability, they target [Eternal Witness] in their graveyard. When Eternal Witness returns to the battlefield, can it target Elspeth Conquers Death with its trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the same: the Saga is sacrificed by state-based actions before the Witness's triggered ability is placed on the stack, so Elspeth Conquers Death is in the graveyard and can be targeted.
entries.answer:
Yes — Eternal Witness's enters-the-battlefield trigger can target the Elspeth Conquers Death card in Alec's graveyard.

Why: Elspeth Conquers Death's chapter III ability ("Return target creature or planeswalker card from your graveyard to the battlefield") returns Eternal Witness. Because the Saga now has lore counters equal to its greatest chapter number, its controller sacrifices it as soon as that chapter ability has left the stack; this state-based action doesn't use the stack [Elspeth Conquers Death ruling #11]. Note also that the chapter ability on the stack is unaffected by the Saga leaving the battlefield [Elspeth Conquers Death ruling #6].

Eternal Witness's ability is a triggered ability, and its target is chosen as the ability is put on the stack, not when it triggers [115.1d]. The sacrifice of Elspeth Conquers Death happens as the chapter ability finishes resolving/leaves the stack, which is before the Eternal Witness trigger is actually put onto the stack and targets are declared. So at the moment Alec chooses the target, the Elspeth Conquers Death card is already in his graveyard and is a legal choice for "target card from your graveyard."

Timing caveat: I'm assuming the normal sequence — chapter III resolves and leaves the stack (Saga sacrificed), then the Eternal Witness trigger is put on the stack with its target chosen. If for some reason Elspeth Conquers Death were still on the battlefield when the target was chosen (for example, if something had removed lore counters so no sacrifice occurred), it wouldn't be in the graveyard and couldn't be targeted; Alec would have to pick a different graveyard card or, since the ability says "you may," simply decline.

Player count doesn't change this; the provided rules and rulings on Sagas and targeting work the same in two-player and multiplayer games (the only multiplayer-specific note given concerns chapter II's cost increase lasting until your next turn if you leave the game [Elspeth Conquers Death ruling #0]).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes.

When the final chapter ability resolves, Eternal Witness is returned to the battlefield. However, its triggered ability is not put onto the stack until after state based actions are checked. When state based actions are checked, Elspeth Conquers Death is sacrificed because is has a number of lore counters greater than or equal to its final chapter number. After this, triggers are placed onto the stack, and Elspeth Conquers Death is in the graveyard able to be the target of Eternal Witness's triggered ability.

entries.question: Autumn attacks with [Robber of the Rich], exiling [Light Up the Stage] from Nehemiah's library. Can Autumn pay Light Up the Stage's Spectacle cost with only {C}?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion — Robber of the Rich lets Autumn spend colorless mana as though it were red, so she can pay Light Up the Stage's {R} spectacle cost with {C} (provided an opponent lost life this turn).
entries.answer:
Yes — Autumn can pay Light Up the Stage's {R} spectacle cost using one {C}, provided an opponent lost life this turn.

Why: Robber of the Rich's ability says that during any turn you attacked with a Rogue, "you may cast that card and you may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." That "as though" effect only changes how Autumn may pay the cost — it does not change the cost itself, and the mana actually spent is still colorless (rule 609.4b). So Light Up the Stage's spectacle cost remains {R} (one red mana), but Autumn may satisfy that {R} symbol with one colorless mana. Note this is specifically the card's granted permission overriding the normal requirement that {R} be paid with red mana.

Spectacle is a static ability functioning on the stack that means "You may pay [cost] rather than pay this spell's mana cost if an opponent lost life this turn" (702.137a). So Autumn still needs an opponent to have lost life this turn — combat damage dealt to Nehemiah by Robber of the Rich would do it, since damage dealt to a player causes that player to lose that much life [Light Up the Stage ruling #4]. Merely exiling the card does not cause life loss. It only matters that an opponent lost life at some point that turn, even if they later gained it back [Light Up the Stage ruling #6], and the spectacle cost is the same regardless of how much life was lost [Light Up the Stage ruling #7].

Timing: Light Up the Stage is a sorcery, and neither Robber of the Rich nor spectacle changes when it can be cast — Autumn must cast it during her own main phase with an empty stack, on a turn she attacked with a Rogue [Robber of the Rich ruling #6], [Light Up the Stage ruling #8], [Robber of the Rich ruling #3]. Casting it removes it from exile, so it can only be cast once [Light Up the Stage ruling #0].

Multiplayer: the answer is the same. "Defending player" for Robber of the Rich's trigger is whoever Robber of the Rich attacked (or the controller of an attacked planeswalker) [Robber of the Rich ruling #9], and spectacle just needs some opponent to have lost life — even one who has since left the game [Light Up the Stage ruling #3].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes.

Robber of the Rich allows Autumn to cast the card and "may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." This changes how the player may pay a cost, and they can do so with any mana, regardless of color. 

"Spectacle" is an alternative cost ([702.137a]), and can only be used if no other alternative cost is being paid. Luckily, Robber of the Rich does not create an alternative cost, it just changes how mana may be spent.

entries.question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Jinx changes Urza's Saga's land type, causing it to lose all chapter abilities and thus be immediately sacrificed under the Urza's Saga ruling/state-based actions.
entries.answer:
Urza's Saga is immediately sacrificed by Nico. Jinx sets Urza's Saga's land subtype to the chosen basic land type (say Island), so under rule 305.7 Urza's Saga loses its old land type (Urza's) and loses all abilities generated from its rules text — that includes its three chapter abilities — while gaining the basic type's mana ability ({T}: Add {U} for Island). Setting a land's subtype doesn't change card types or supertypes (205.4b), so it is still an enchantment land and still has the enchantment subtype Saga (Saga is an enchantment subtype, not a land type, so Jinx doesn't strip it).

That leaves a Saga permanent with no chapter abilities. Rule 704.5s / 714.4 makes a Saga's controller sacrifice it when its lore counters are at or above its final chapter number and it isn't the source of a chapter ability on the stack; with no chapter abilities at all, the Urza's Saga ruling covers it directly: if Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, it is immediately sacrificed [Urza's Saga ruling #1]. This is a state-based action that doesn't use the stack, so it happens as soon as Jinx finishes resolving — the two lore counters don't matter.

Note that abilities granted to the land by other effects survive rule 305.7, so any ability Urza's Saga had already gained from its chapter I or chapter II triggers would in principle stay — but since Urza's Saga is sacrificed right away, that's moot. Alexzander still draws a card at the beginning of the next turn's upkeep from Jinx.

This works the same regardless of the number of players; only Nico, as Urza's Saga's controller, sacrifices it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
In layer 4, Urza's Saga will have its land type overwritten as well as lose all of its chapter abilities. It will gain the abilities to tap for {C} and to create Construct tokens in layer 6, as those abilities are granted by a continuous effect that was generated when the previous chapter abilities resolved..

Because Urza's Saga has lost all of its chapter abilities while still being a Saga, it is immediately sacrificed the next time state-based actions are checked, per the Urza's Saga ruling "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed".

entries.question: Ada controls [Ethersworn Canonist]. They want to suspend [Shade of Trokair] and then cast [Divination]. Can they?
entries.reason: Both conclude suspending is not casting and so does not count toward Ethersworn Canonist, allowing Ada to suspend Shade of Trokair and then cast Divination.
entries.answer:
Yes, assuming Ada hasn't already cast a nonartifact spell this turn and it's their main phase with an empty stack.

Why: exiling a card with suspend is a special action, not casting a spell ([116.2f], [Shade of Trokair ruling #7]). So paying {W} to exile Shade of Trokair with three time counters does not make Ada a player who "has cast a nonartifact spell this turn" for Ethersworn Canonist. Ethersworn Canonist only shuts off *additional* nonartifact spells after one has been cast, so Divination (a nonartifact sorcery) is still Ada's one permitted nonartifact spell for the turn ([Ethersworn Canonist ruling #1]).

Timing requirement for the suspend action: Ada may take it only if they could begin to cast Shade of Trokair by putting it on the stack from their hand ([116.2f], [702.62a]), and effects that prohibit casting it are taken into account ([702.62c], [601.3], [Shade of Trokair ruling #2]). Shade of Trokair is a creature card, so that means during Ada's main phase with an empty stack while they have priority ([117.1a]). Crucially, if Ada had already cast a nonartifact spell earlier this turn, Ethersworn Canonist would prohibit casting Shade of Trokair, and therefore Ada could not suspend it either — so do the suspending first, then cast Divination, not the reverse.

Also note: when the last time counter is later removed, the suspend trigger lets Ada cast Shade of Trokair ignoring normal timing permissions ([702.62a], [Shade of Trokair ruling #5]) — but Ethersworn Canonist would still stop that cast on a turn Ada has already cast a nonartifact spell, since that cast is a real cast.

Multiplayer: no difference. Ethersworn Canonist applies per player, and the suspend action and casting rules used here are the same regardless of the number of players; the provided rules contain nothing player-count-dependent for this interaction.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Suspending a card is not casting a spell, so it does not count towards Ethersworn Canonist's restriction.

entries.question: Asa controls an [Inventors' Fair], a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], and two [Piston Sledge]. They want to activate the last ability of Inventors' Fair and sacrifice a Piston Sledge to help pay the cost. Is this legal?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling — the Fair's activation is legal and Asa may sacrifice a Piston Sledge to Krark‑Clan Ironworks (after activation) to produce mana used toward paying the Fair's cost.
entries.answer:
Yes, it's legal — but only indirectly: Asa can't sacrifice a Piston Sledge "to" Inventors' Fair's ability, because that ability's cost is "{4}, {T}, Sacrifice Inventors' Fair" and contains no sacrifice-an-artifact component. What Asa can do is activate Krark-Clan Ironworks' mana ability, sacrificing a Piston Sledge, to make {C}{C}, and spend that {C}{C} toward the {4} generic portion (generic mana is payable with colorless mana).

Details:

1. Legality check on activation: Inventors' Fair's ability says "Activate only if you control three or more artifacts." As Asa activates it, Asa controls Krark-Clan Ironworks and two Piston Sledge — exactly three artifacts, so the requirement is met (Inventors' Fair itself is a land, not an artifact). Per [Inventors' Fair ruling #2], the artifact count is checked only as the ability is activated, not again on resolution, so sacrificing a Piston Sledge afterward doesn't invalidate anything.

2. Timing of the Krark-Clan Ironworks activation: mana abilities may be activated whenever a player is in the middle of casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment [605.3a], so Asa may activate Krark-Clan Ironworks after Inventors' Fair's ability is on the stack and its total cost is locked in, during payment [601.2h].

3. One sacrifice = one cost: sacrificing that Piston Sledge pays Krark-Clan Ironworks' cost and nothing else; it does not also pay any part of Inventors' Fair's cost [118.10]. Its only contribution is the {C}{C} produced.

4. Remaining cost: {C}{C} covers 2 of the {4}. Asa still needs 2 more generic mana from other sources, plus tapping and sacrificing Inventors' Fair itself. Note Inventors' Fair's own "{T}: Add {C}" cannot help here, since the {T} in the search ability's cost requires it to be untapped and it can only be tapped once [118.3]. If Asa can't produce the remaining 2 generic mana, the cost is unpayable — partial payments aren't allowed and the game rewinds to before the activation [601.2h].

The second Piston Sledge can likewise be fed to Krark-Clan Ironworks for another {C}{C} if needed, since the artifact-count restriction was already satisfied at activation.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count; it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The process for activating an ability is the same as the process for casting a spell. It must be legal to activate the ability in order to put it onto the stack. Mana abilities are only activated after the legality of activating the original ability has been checked.

entries.question: Amare controls [Psychogenic Probe] and casts [Pain], targeting Nico. They discard a [Progenitus]. Does Psychogenic Probe trigger?
entries.reason: Both conclude Progenitus's replacement effect turns the discard into a shuffle, which satisfies Psychogenic Probe's trigger so it triggers (dealing 2 damage to Nico).
entries.answer:
Yes. Psychogenic Probe triggers and deals 2 damage to Nico.

Why: Progenitus has the ability "If Progenitus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Progenitus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." That is a replacement ability on Progenitus, so when Nico discards Progenitus to Pain, Progenitus is never put into the graveyard — instead an ability causes Nico to shuffle their library. Psychogenic Probe reads "Whenever a spell or ability causes a player to shuffle their library, this artifact deals 2 damage to that player," and Progenitus's ability is exactly such an ability, so the trigger condition is actually met and the ability triggers ([603.2g] — a trigger event must actually occur, and here it does). The 2 damage is dealt to Nico, the player who shuffled.

A few clarifications:
- Progenitus's "protection from everything" is irrelevant here: the damage is dealt to Nico, not to Progenitus, and Psychogenic Probe doesn't target Progenitus ([Progenitus ruling #0], [Progenitus ruling #1]).
- Pain is one half of the split card Pain // Suffering; you cast one half, and while the spell is on the stack the other half's characteristics are ignored ([Pain // Suffering ruling #5], [Pain // Suffering ruling #6]). Casting Pain targeting Nico, an opponent, is also a "crime" if anything cares ([700.13], [Crime]).
- Psychogenic Probe would even trigger if Nico's library were empty when the shuffle happens ([Psychogenic Probe ruling #0]).
- Timing note: the trigger happens when the discard/replacement actually occurs during Pain's resolution, not when Pain is cast; Psychogenic Probe's triggered ability then goes on the stack and resolves after Pain finishes resolving.

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — the damage simply goes to whichever player shuffled (Nico), regardless of player count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Progenitus's replacement effect changes the effect of Pain from "Nico discards a card, putting it into their graveyard" to "Nico reveals a card and shuffles it into their library". Pain still caused the shuffle, so Psychogenic Probe triggers.

entries.question: Albert controls [Doubling Season] and [Pir, Imaginative Rascal] and activates the +1 ability of [Ajani, Mentor of Heroes]. How many loyalty counters does it gain?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Ajani gains 2 counters while the correct ruling is 4, so the candidate's final conclusion contradicts the reference.
entries.answer:
Ajani, Mentor of Heroes gains 2 loyalty counters, not 4.

Why: the [+1] is a cost paid as you activate the loyalty ability, not something an effect does. Doubling Season reads "If an effect would put one or more counters on a permanent you control..." and [Doubling Season ruling #4] states explicitly that loyalty counters put on as an activation cost are NOT doubled, because they're a cost rather than an effect. So Doubling Season doesn't apply here.

Pir, Imaginative Rascal's second ability is worded differently: "If one or more counters would be put on a permanent your team controls, that many plus one of each of those kinds of counters are put on that permanent instead." It is not limited to counters put on by an effect, so it applies to the loyalty counter paid as a cost, and Albert puts 1 + 1 = 2 loyalty counters on Ajani, Mentor of Heroes. Compare [606.5], which likewise treats extra loyalty-counter costs as being combined into the single cost actually paid.

Separately, the +1/+1 counters the ability distributes ARE from an effect, so both replacement effects apply there: Albert distributes three +1/+1 counters as announced ([Ajani, Mentor of Heroes ruling #1]), and for each creature receiving counters Albert chooses the order of Pir, Imaginative Rascal and Doubling Season ([616.1g]). Applying Pir, Imaginative Rascal first then Doubling Season on a creature slated for 1 counter gives (1+1)×2 = 4; Doubling Season first gives (1×2)+1 = 3. Pir, Imaginative Rascal applies separately to each distribution instruction ([Pir, Imaginative Rascal ruling #4]).

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games (Pir, Imaginative Rascal's "your team" matters only in team formats such as Two-Headed Giant).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Four.

Activating a planeswalker ability includes paying the loyalty cost, which in this case means adding one loyalty counter. Doubling Season only replaces effects, which are the result of a spell or ability. However Pir, Imaginative Rascal replaces the original one loyalty counter with two, which Doubling Season can then replace with doubling the additional loyalty counters, resulting in a total of four.

entries.question: Aminah casts a [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Aminah chooses to put a [Haru-Onna] onto the battlefield and Nico chooses to put a [Domestication] onto the battlefield enchanting Haru-Onna. Who controls the enters-the-battlefield ability of Haru-Onna?
entries.reason: The reference says Nico cannot legally choose Domestication to enchant a permanent entering via Show and Tell, so the candidate's conclusion that Nico controls Haru-Onna's ETB trigger is incorrect.
entries.answer:
Nico controls Haru-Onna's enters-the-battlefield trigger, so Nico draws the card.

Why: Show and Tell has each player choose in turn order (Aminah, the active player, first), but the chosen cards are then put onto the battlefield *simultaneously* [Show and Tell ruling #2]. So Domestication enters already attached to Haru-Onna, and its continuous control-changing effect ("You control enchanted creature") is applied immediately as a layer 2 effect when the game state is checked [613.1b]. Although Haru-Onna would by default enter under Aminah's control as the player the effect put it onto the battlefield [110.2a], the control-changing effect from Nico's Domestication means Nico controls Haru-Onna from the moment it's on the battlefield. Note that an Aura's controller and the enchanted creature's controller are tracked separately [303.4e] — here they happen to be the same player, Nico.

Haru-Onna's ability ("When this creature enters, draw a card") is a triggered ability, and a triggered ability is controlled by the player who controlled its source at the time it triggered [603.3a], [113.8], [109.4b]. Since Nico controls Haru-Onna at that moment, Nico puts the trigger on the stack and "you" in "draw a card" refers to Nico.

Aminah still owns the Haru-Onna card [110.2a], which matters for its other ability ("return this creature to its owner's hand") and if Haru-Onna later leaves and returns, but ownership doesn't affect who controls the trigger.

Timing note: this assumes both cards genuinely hit the battlefield simultaneously from the same Show and Tell resolution, which is what the card does. If instead Domestication arrived later (e.g., cast separately after Haru-Onna's trigger had already triggered), Aminah would have controlled the trigger and drawn the card.

Multiplayer: the answer is the same with more than two players — every player gets the option under Show and Tell, choices are made in turn order starting with the active player [Show and Tell ruling #0], and whoever's Domestication ends up controlling Haru-Onna as it enters controls the draw trigger.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. Nico must choose a permanent that is already on the battlefield for the Domestication to enchant. They can't choose a permanent that is entering at the same time.

entries.question:
Amani controls a [Founding the Third Path], and its third ability is resolving. Amani chooses to cast a [Fatal Push] from their graveyard. Amani currently does not have Revolt.
Can Amani choose to target [Skyhunter Patrol] with Fatal Push? Will Skyhunter Patrol be destroyed by Fatal Push?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly concludes Skyhunter Patrol won't be destroyed—unlike the reference, it fails to account that the saga is sacrificed (giving Revolt) before Fatal Push resolves, so the Push will destroy the Patrol.
entries.answer:
Yes, Amani can target Skyhunter Patrol, but Skyhunter Patrol will not be destroyed.

Targeting: Fatal Push says "Destroy target creature if it has mana value 2 or less." The mana value condition is not a targeting restriction — Fatal Push can target any creature, even one with mana value 5 or greater, and the mana value is checked only as Fatal Push resolves [Fatal Push ruling #3]. Skyhunter Patrol is a creature on the battlefield, so it's a legal target [115.2].

Resolution: Skyhunter Patrol's mana cost is {2}{W}{W}, so its mana value is 4. Without Revolt (no permanent left the battlefield under Amani's control this turn), Fatal Push only destroys the target if its mana value is 2 or less. Skyhunter Patrol still is a legal target, so Fatal Push resolves normally [608.2b], but the destroy condition isn't met and nothing happens to Skyhunter Patrol. Had Revolt been satisfied, the threshold would be mana value 4 or less and Skyhunter Patrol would be destroyed.

Mechanics of the cast: chapter III of Founding the Third Path exiles the Fatal Push card from Amani's graveyard, creates a copy, and lets Amani cast the copy. Amani must cast it right then, during the resolution of that ability, and must pay all of its costs — that is {B}; this is not a "without paying its mana cost" effect [Founding the Third Path ruling #2].

If Skyhunter Patrol is controlled by an opponent, casting Fatal Push targeting it is committing a crime [700.13][Crime]. That works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — any opponent's permanent counts.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes Amani can target Skyhunter Patrol, and it will be destroyed by Fatal Push.

Fatal Push does not check for the target's mana value when put on the stack, so Amani is allowed to target Skyhunter Patrol.

Amani will put Fatal Push on the stack as part of the resolution of Founding the Third Path's third chapter. Once the ability is done resolving, SBAs are checked and the saga is sacrificed. In particular this means that Amani will have Revolt when Fatal Push resolves, thus Skyhunter Patrol will get destroyed.

entries.question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling: Titania's Song makes Soldevi Digger a 2/2 artifact creature with no abilities (losing Equipment status), so Bludgeon Brawl no longer applies to it.
entries.answer:
Soldevi Digger becomes a colorless 2/2 artifact creature named Soldevi Digger with no abilities — no Equipment subtype, no equip ability, no "{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library," and it is not attached to anything.

Why: Titania's Song says each noncreature artifact loses all abilities and becomes an artifact creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value. Soldevi Digger's mana cost is {2}, so its mana value is 2, making it 2/2. Its mana cost, name, and color (colorless) are unchanged — Titania's Song doesn't touch those characteristics (see rule 109.3 for the list of characteristics).

Bludgeon Brawl stops applying to it. Bludgeon Brawl only affects each noncreature, non-Equipment artifact; once Titania's Song makes Soldevi Digger a creature, it no longer meets that description. Per [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #2], that artifact stops being an Equipment and becomes unattached from any creature it was attached to, while remaining on the battlefield. So if Soldevi Digger had been equipped to a creature, it falls off. This is also consistent with [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #3]: an Equipment that's also a creature can't be equipped to anything.

On layers: continuous effects are applied in layers starting from the printed values (rule 613.1a), and an effect whose parts belong in different layers applies each part in its own layer (rule 613.6) — Titania's Song's type change in layer 4, its ability removal in layer 6, and its power/toughness setting in layer 7b. Because Bludgeon Brawl's effect depends on whether the artifact is a noncreature non-Equipment artifact, it simply has nothing to apply to here; the ruling above is decisive.

One practical note from [Titania's Song ruling #0]: even though Soldevi Digger is now a creature, it can only attack if Ari has continuously controlled it since the beginning of their most recent turn — how long it's been a creature doesn't matter. (Its {T} abilities are moot since it has none left.)

Also note Titania's Song's own text: if Titania's Song later leaves the battlefield, its effect continues until end of turn, so Soldevi Digger stays a 2/2 ability-less creature for the rest of that turn and only then can Bludgeon Brawl make it an Equipment again.

Nothing here depends on player count, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It's a 2/2 artifact creature with no abilities. Applying Titania's Song would cause Bludgeon Brawl to no longer apply (since Soldevi Digger would be a creature). However, applying Bludgeon Brawl would not change how Titania's Song's effect is applied, so Bludgeon Brawl is dependent on Titania's Song. Titania's Song applies first, and then Bludgeon Brawl won't affect Soldevi Digger since it's a creature.

entries.question: Audrey casts [Enlarge] targeting [Goblin Piker], and then attacks with the Goblin Piker. Nico blocks it with a [Baron Sengir], which has gained infect due to their [Grafted Exoskeleton] and indestructible due to their [Withstand Death]. What happens at the end of the turn?
entries.reason: Both conclude Enlarge ends and the -1/-1 counters remain, causing Goblin Piker to die at cleanup and triggering Baron Sengir's ability.
entries.answer:
At end of turn, Goblin Piker dies, and Baron Sengir survives.

During combat (assuming Goblin Piker is blocked by Baron Sengir, as Enlarge requires if able):
- Goblin Piker is 2/1 plus Enlarge's +7/+7 = 9/8 with trample; Baron Sengir is 5/5 plus Grafted Exoskeleton's +2/+2 = 7/7 with infect and (from Withstand Death) indestructible.
- Baron Sengir has infect, so its 7 combat damage isn't marked on Goblin Piker; instead Nico puts seven -1/-1 counters on Goblin Piker [702.90c]. Those counters are applied in layer 7 along with Enlarge's +7/+7, so Goblin Piker is 2/1 at that moment and doesn't die yet.
- Goblin Piker's damage to Baron Sengir is just marked damage; Baron Sengir is indestructible, so it isn't destroyed. Any excess trample damage to Nico is ordinary damage (Goblin Piker doesn't have infect), so it's life loss, not poison counters.
- The -1/-1 counters stay on Goblin Piker permanently — they aren't removed at end of turn [Grafted Exoskeleton ruling #6].

Then, in the cleanup step, all damage marked on permanents is removed and all "until end of turn" effects end simultaneously [514.2]. That means Enlarge's +7/+7 and Withstand Death's indestructible both wear off, and Baron Sengir's marked damage is removed. Goblin Piker is now 2/1 base with seven -1/-1 counters still on it, i.e. -5/-6 [613.1g]. Because its toughness is 0 or less, the state-based action check puts it into its owner's graveyard [704.5f]; indestructible wouldn't have saved it anyway, and neither would regeneration [704.5f].

Baron Sengir is unaffected: it's back to 7/7 (5/5 plus Grafted Exoskeleton) with no damage marked, so losing indestructible costs it nothing.

Because Goblin Piker was dealt damage by Baron Sengir this turn and then dies, Baron Sengir's triggered ability ("Whenever a creature dealt damage by Baron Sengir this turn dies, put a +2/+2 counter on Baron Sengir") meets its trigger condition. The rules provided here don't include the cleanup-step rule governing abilities that trigger during cleanup, so I can't cite chapter and verse for the exact handling; note only that state-based actions don't wait for triggers [704.4].

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same with two players or more, except that in a multiplayer game Nico is whichever player was chosen as the defending player, and only that player takes the trample damage.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The effect from Enlarge wears off, but the -1/-1 counters on Goblin Piker remain. Goblin Piker dies. It was dealt damage that turn by Baron Sengir, so Baron Sengir triggers.

entries.question: Niko has a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] in their graveyard with 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Ashley controls [Containment Priest], and casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Niko. What happens?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude that Skullbriar is exiled (prevented from entering by Containment Priest), retains its +1/+1 counters in exile, and nothing ends up on the battlefield.
entries.answer:
Nothing ends up on the battlefield: every creature card exiled from Niko's graveyard by Ghastly Conscription is exiled again by Containment Priest as it tries to be manifested, including Skullbriar, the Walking Grave.

Step by step:

1. Ghastly Conscription exiles all creature cards from Niko's graveyard in a face-down pile, shuffles that pile, then manifests those cards — i.e., tries to put each onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature.
2. Manifesting is not casting, and each of those cards is a nontoken card that would enter as a creature. Containment Priest reads "If a nontoken creature would enter and it wasn't cast, exile it instead," so each one is exiled instead of entering. [Containment Priest ruling #1] confirms the ability only spares creatures that were actually cast, and [Containment Priest ruling #3] confirms that what matters is whether the object would enter as a creature — a manifested card would, since manifest makes it a 2/2 creature.
3. Because Containment Priest's exile is a replacement effect on entering the battlefield, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave never actually enters the battlefield, so it is never a face-down 2/2 permanent, no "enters" triggers occur, and Niko has no chance to turn it face up for its mana cost as a special action ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #2]).
4. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's counters: its third ability says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library," and [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1] says the ability works if Skullbriar has it in the zone it's moving from. In Niko's graveyard it has that ability, so the 2 +1/+1 counters travel with it into exile with the rest of the pile. It then moves exile-to-exile via Containment Priest's replacement, and per [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #5] it retains all counters it has. So Skullbriar, the Walking Grave sits in exile as a 3/3 card (counters change its power/toughness even outside the battlefield, per [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2]).
5. Reminder from [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #3]: any "for as long as it has a counter" effects don't carry over — it's a new object in each new zone.

One assumption worth naming: I'm assuming Containment Priest is already on the battlefield when Ghastly Conscription resolves (it has flash, so Ashley could also flash it in earlier). If Containment Priest instead entered the battlefield simultaneously with those manifested cards, it would not affect them ([Containment Priest ruling #2]) — but that can't happen here, since Ghastly Conscription's manifests happen on resolution while Containment Priest is already out.

Player count doesn't matter here: Ghastly Conscription targets one player (Niko), and Containment Priest's replacement applies regardless of who controls the entering creature, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: In order for counters to remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, it needs to have that ability immediately before it changes zones. It did have that ability in the graveyard, so it is exiled face down with the +1/+1 counters remaining on it during that change. It then attempts to enter the battlefield, but remains in exile instead due to Containment Priest. Since it becomes a new object, it will be face-up in exile. However it didn't change zones, so the counters will remain on it in exile.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Skill Borrower] and [Sensei's Divining Top]. The top card of their library is a [Putrid Leech]. Ashley activates Skill Borrower's ability, then activates Sensei's Divining Top's first ability, choosing to put Putrid Leech second from the top. Then they activate Sensei's Divining Top again, putting Putrid Leech back on top. Can Ashley activate Skill Borrower's ability again?
entries.reason: Both conclude Ashley can activate it again because Putrid Leech stopped being revealed and became a new object, so Skill Borrower gains a new instance of the granted activated ability not subject to the earlier "activate only once each turn" restriction.
entries.answer:
Yes — Ashley can activate the pumped-up "Pay 2 life: This creature gets +2/+2 until end of turn" ability a second time this turn.

Here's why. Skill Borrower says "Play with the top card of your library revealed" and grants Skill Borrower all activated abilities of that top card while it's an artifact or creature card, so with Putrid Leech on top Skill Borrower has "Pay 2 life: This creature gets +2/+2 until end of turn. Activate only once each turn."

When Ashley uses Sensei's Divining Top's first ability ({1}: Look at the top three cards of your library, then put them back in any order) to bury Putrid Leech second from the top, Putrid Leech stops being the revealed top card. When the second activation of Sensei's Divining Top puts Putrid Leech back on top, rule 401.6 applies: a card that stops being revealed for any length of time before being revealed again becomes a new object. So the Putrid Leech now on top is a different object from the one Skill Borrower drew the ability from earlier, and Skill Borrower's granted ability is a newly acquired ability.

Rule 602.5c is the key: when an object acquires an activated ability that carries a restriction on its use, that restriction applies only to that ability as acquired from that object, and not to other, identically worded abilities. The "Activate only once each turn" restriction attached to the first-acquired instance doesn't carry over to the instance acquired from the new object, so Skill Borrower may activate it again this turn (paying 2 more life).

Timing note: I'm assuming Ashley's first Skill Borrower activation happened while the original Putrid Leech was still the top card and fully resolved (or at least was activated) before the first Sensei's Divining Top activation. If Ashley instead activated the granted ability while the top card was changing, note rule 401.5 (the new top card isn't revealed until the activation is complete) and Skill Borrower ruling #4: the ability still resolves normally even though Skill Borrower has lost it.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since only Ashley's own library and permanents are involved.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Putrid Leech stopped being revealed for a time, so it is no longer the same object that it was before. Skill Borrower has a new ability that just has the same text as the ability that was activated earlier.

entries.question: Noah controls a [Mons's Goblin Raiders] enchanted with a [Spider Umbra]. Alexandra casts [Yamabushi's Flame], targeting Mons's Goblin Raiders. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion and reasoning: Spider Umbra's replacement prevents the creature from being destroyed (the Aura is destroyed instead), so Yamabushi's Flame's exile replacement doesn't apply and nothing is exiled.
entries.answer:
Mons's Goblin Raiders survives; Spider Umbra is destroyed instead, and nothing is exiled.

Details: Spider Umbra makes Mons's Goblin Raiders a 2/2. Yamabushi's Flame deals 3 damage to it, which is lethal, so the game's lethal-damage state-based action would destroy Mons's Goblin Raiders. Umbra armor — "If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura" [702.89a] — replaces that destruction: all damage is removed from Mons's Goblin Raiders and Spider Umbra goes to Noah's graveyard. This is mandatory, not optional [Spider Umbra ruling #6], and it applies regardless of whether the destruction came from lethal damage or a "destroy" effect [Spider Umbra ruling #4]. Note that with lethal damage it's the game rules, not Yamabushi's Flame, that cause Spider Umbra to be destroyed [Spider Umbra ruling #0].

Because Mons's Goblin Raiders never dies, Yamabushi's Flame's replacement clause ("If a creature dealt damage this way would die this turn, exile it instead") does nothing here — it only applies if that creature would actually die. Once Spider Umbra leaves, Mons's Goblin Raiders is back to 1/1 with no damage marked on it, so it doesn't then die; the damage was removed, not merely reduced. Also, umbra armor is not regeneration, so Mons's Goblin Raiders isn't tapped or removed from combat [Spider Umbra ruling #3].

One caution for the rest of the turn: Yamabushi's Flame's exile effect lasts all turn for a creature it damaged, but since the damage was removed and Mons's Goblin Raiders survived, it's only relevant if that creature would die later this turn — and it would then be exiled rather than going to the graveyard, with no umbra armor left to save it.

This interaction doesn't depend on the number of players, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Spider Umbra is destroyed and Mons's Goblin Raiders remains on the battlefield.

There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the same event. Umbra armor is attempting to replace the destruction of the creature, while Yamabushi's Flame's effect is attempting to replace where the creature moves to. The "move to the graveyard" event is a part of the "destroy" event, so the umbra armor replacement effect must apply first. Once that effect has been applied, the creature is no longer about to die, so there are no more effects to apply.

If the Mons's Goblin Raiders would die later in the turn, the Yamabushi's Flame's replacement effect will apply at that time and cause it to move to exile instead of the graveyard.

entries.question: At the beginning of the game, Alex announced [Kaheera, the Orphanguard] as their companion. During the game, Alex cast [Carrion Grub] from their sideboard with [Wish]. Later, Alex restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate makes Kaheera's status conditional (depending on whether its {3} cost was paid) and leaves open whether it can be re‑announced, while the reference definitively states Carrion Grub is shuffled into the deck and therefore Kaheera cannot be announced as the companion.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: Carrion Grub, which Alex brought in from outside the game with Wish, becomes part of Alex's deck/library for the new game — it is shuffled in as the new game starts and is no longer a sideboard card. Kaheera, the Orphanguard's fate depends on whether Alex had already paid {3} to put it into their hand before the restart.

Why Carrion Grub is in the library: when a game is restarted, all Magic cards involved in the game that ended are involved in the new game, even if they weren't originally part of it, and ownership doesn't change. The rules give exactly this example: a card brought in from outside the game (via a wish-style effect) is part of that player's library when the new game begins [727.2]. Note also that players can't otherwise shuffle cards between deck and sideboard before the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #5], and the new game starts with a normal pregame procedure — shuffle, life totals reset, seven-card hands, mulligans allowed [Karn Liberated ruling #9], with Alex as starting player.

Kaheera, the Orphanguard, two cases:
- If Alex had already paid {3} and taken the special action to put Kaheera, the Orphanguard into their hand, that card is in the game and remains in the game until the game ends [702.139c, Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #14]. Since it was involved in the game that ended, it is involved in the new game and, like Carrion Grub, will be in Alex's library after the restart [727.2] — so it is no longer available as a companion outside the game.
- If Alex never paid the {3}, Kaheera, the Orphanguard was still outside the game (sideboard) and was never "involved in the game," so 727.2 doesn't pull it into the new library; it stays outside the game. The provided rules do not explicitly state whether Alex may re-announce a companion for the restarted game, and the pregame companion reveal happens before shuffling [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #0]. Treat that specific point as unsettled by the rules given.

One wrinkle: with Carrion Grub now in Alex's deck, if Alex does get a companion for the new game, Kaheera, the Orphanguard's requirement (every creature card in the starting deck is a Cat, Elemental, Nightmare, Dinosaur, or Beast) would fail, because Carrion Grub is an Insect [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #2].

Timing/sequence assumption: I'm assuming Wish resolved and Carrion Grub was actually cast and thus in the game (graveyard, battlefield, wherever) when Karn Liberated's −14 resolved. If Carrion Grub had never actually been brought into the game, it would simply have stayed in the sideboard.

Also, none of the game's history carries over [Karn Liberated ruling #1], any non-Aura permanent cards exiled with Karn Liberated's first two abilities stay exiled and are put onto the battlefield under Alex's control just before the first untap step [727.4, Karn Liberated ruling #4, Karn Liberated ruling #6].

Multiplayer note: with more than two players, every player still in the game when it restarted joins the new game, and Alex is the starting player [727.1, 727.7, Karn Liberated ruling #9]; any player who had already left the game before the restart is not in the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #11]. Otherwise the answer above is the same at any table size.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Carrion Grub will be shuffled into Alex's library along with the rest of the cards in the game. Because Carrion Grub violates Kaheera, the Orphanguard's companion restriction, Alex can't announce it as their companion for the restarted game.
